questions.q: Using the method 'Mean of a Data Set', work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mean.
Take the relation taught for 'Mean of a Data Set' and work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mean.
Explain in your own words what 'Mean of a Data Set' refers to.
questions.a: The mean is the plain average of a numeric attribute: add all the values and divide by how many there are; it summarises a whole column of a table in one number but gets distorted by outliers.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Mean of a Data Set'.
questions.a: The nine student heights [90, 102, 110, 115, 85, 90, 100, 110, 110] give a mean of about 101.33 cm.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Mean of a Data Set', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: mean = total / count

questions.q: Using the method 'Median Position in Sorted Values', work with: count = 150. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of below_count.
questions.a: 74.5 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Median Position in Sorted Values' and work with: count = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of below_count.
questions.a: 149.5 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Median Position in Sorted Values' refers to.
questions.a: The median is the central value once the data are sorted; with an odd count of n values it sits at position n plus 1 over 2, and with an even count it is the average of the two middle values.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Median Position in Sorted Values'.
questions.a: Sorting [90, 102, 110, 115, 85, 90, 100, 110, 110] puts 102 exactly in the fifth of nine positions.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Median Position in Sorted Values', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: mid_slot = (count + 1) / 2

questions.q: Find the range of the height data whose smallest value is 85 cm and largest is 115 cm.. Use the method 'Range between Extremes'. Work with: largest = 25, smallest = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mid_range.
questions.a: 32.5 units

questions.q: Compute the midrange of a data set spanning 85 to 115.. Use the method 'Range between Extremes'. Work with: largest = 24, smallest = 360. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mid_range.
questions.a: 192 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Range between Extremes' refers to.
questions.a: The range measures spread using only the two extreme values: the largest minus the smallest, so a single outlier can inflate it; the midpoint of that span is called the midrange.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Range between Extremes'.
questions.a: Heights from 85 cm to 115 cm span a range of 30 cm centred on the midrange 100 cm.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Range between Extremes', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: range = largest - smallest

questions.q: Using the method 'Standard Deviation of the Data', work with: count = 50, sum_sq = 120. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of sd.
questions.a: 1.5492 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Standard Deviation of the Data' and work with: count = 20, sum_sq = 60. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of sd.
questions.a: 1.7321 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Standard Deviation of the Data' refers to.
questions.a: Standard deviation measures how widely values stray from the mean: subtract the mean from each value, square the differences, average them, and take the positive square root; a small value means tightly packed data.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Standard Deviation of the Data'.
questions.a: The nine heights give squared deviations totalling 938, so the variance is about 104.22 and the standard deviation about 10.21 cm.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Standard Deviation of the Data', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: sd = sqrt(sum_of_squared_deviations / count)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Mode as Highest Frequency' refers to.
questions.a: The mode is the value occurring most often in the data; a set where every value appears once has no mode, and several values tying at the top frequency make the data multi-modal.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Mode as Highest Frequency'.
questions.a: In the height data, 110 appears three times, more than any other value, so 110 is the mode.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Mode as Highest Frequency', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: mode -> value with maximum frequency

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Structured and Unstructured Data' refers to.
questions.a: Structured data fits a fixed rows-and-columns layout where each column is an attribute and each row an observation, like the kitchen inventory table; unstructured data, such as newspaper pages, emails or videos, follows no fixed record format.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Structured and Unstructured Data'.
questions.a: Summing the Items_in_Inventory column works only because the data are structured.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Structured and Unstructured Data', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: rows x columns with named attributes -> structured

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Metadata: Data about Data' refers to.
questions.a: Metadata describes other data rather than carrying the content itself: an email's subject, recipient and attachment list, or an image's size, format and resolution, all help programs organise the underlying data.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Metadata: Data about Data'.
questions.a: A photo taken on a phone carries metadata such as image size, JPEG or PNG type and resolution.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Metadata: Data about Data', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: metadata = subject, size, type, resolution of the content

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Data Processing Cycle' refers to.
questions.a: Raw data becomes decisions through a cycle: collect the data, prepare and enter it, store it on devices such as HDD, SSD or pen drive, process it, and publish the output as reports, tables or charts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Data Processing Cycle'.
questions.a: An ATM withdrawal shows the cycle at work: PIN and amount enter, the system verifies and debits, and a printed slip comes out.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Data Processing Cycle', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: collection -> preparation -> entry -> storage -> processing -> output
